frase_gancho.texto: A stone figure that seems about to move, caught in a moment three thousand years ago.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the instant we move on to the mystery. Look for a seated young man holding a sleeping child with jaguar features in his arms: the most famous green stone work of the Olmec.

guion_corto.texto: This dark basalt sculpture measures about sixty-six centimeters and was found in Antonio Plaza, near the Uxpanapa River, in Veracruz. It is called “the Wrestler” because of its posture, although we do not know for certain what it represents. He sits on the ground, with his legs bent and his torso turned to one side, as he raises both arms, bent. His head is shaved, and he has a mustache and a trimmed beard. What is surprising is the movement: almost all the sculptures of its time are rigid and frontal; this one, by contrast, seems to capture a single instant. Notice how the muscles of the chest and back tense. It is one of the great masterpieces of ancient sculpture in the Americas.

guion_largo.texto:
Try this: walk slowly around this sculpture. Each side offers a different figure, and that is its first lesson: it was designed to be seen from every angle, not just from the front, like almost all the sculptures of its time. The Olmec artist wanted the viewer to walk around it and, in doing so, to see the body turn.

The name is misleading. It was called “the Wrestler” because its posture recalls a wrestler in the middle of a maneuver. But we do not know whether he was one, or whether he is a priest, a ball player or a dignitary, or what he was doing. Specialists have proposed several ideas; none is definitive. Perhaps it was not an action: perhaps it was a moment in a ritual, a dance turn or the moment of a trance.

Look at the head. It is shaved, and the face has a mustache and a trimmed beard. In Mesoamerica, men tended to have little facial hair, and that is why figures with beards are rare; it is thought that this signaled maturity and rank. It is an individual face, that of someone with a name and a life story, not a generic type.

Now look at the body. The collarbones, the pectoral muscles and the spine are sculpted with a smoothness that almost makes you forget it is hard stone. The torso leans, the shoulders turn, the arms rise, bent: there is tension, there is strength, there is balance. Whoever made it observed real bodies. And did so without metal tools: with harder stones and with sand, with the same patience with which the [rock crystal cup](mna_s07_copa_cristal_roca) from Oaxaca was carved. Just imagine how many days, or perhaps months, of slow wearing down were needed to achieve a single curve of the shoulder.

This piece tells us something important: Olmec art is not only giant heads. Alongside the cold power of the colossal heads, there is a naturalism capable of capturing movement. Several centuries before Greek sculptors polished their athletes in marble, someone in the jungle of southern Veracruz had already achieved a body in tension.

One more detail about the place where it was found. It was not in the great Olmec centers, San Lorenzo or La Venta, but far from them, deep in the jungle. It is a reminder that Olmec territory was vast, and that beneath the vegetation there are still pieces waiting to be found.

And now, a challenge for your body. Try to imitate its posture: legs bent, torso turned, arms bent and raised high. You will see that it is not easy to hold it even for a minute. The sculptor made the stone seem to do it effortlessly, and that, more than strength, is what makes him a master.

Compare it with [the Danzantes](mna_s07_danzante_montealban) of Monte Albán, which you saw a few minutes ago. Those bodies were limp, inert, the bodies of the defeated. This one is the opposite: a living body, in full control of itself. Two opposite ways of representing the human body, and both of them in stone.

texto: Walk around the sculpture: how does the figure change from each side?
Find the beard and the mustache
Notice the turn of the torso and how the arms tense

texto.Origin: Antonio Plaza, municipality of Jesús Carranza, Veracruz
texto.Dimensions: 0.66 m tall x 0.40 m wide x 0.42 m thick
texto.Discovery: Found by chance in 1933 by a farmer who was plowing the land

texto.pregunta: Myth: Olmec sculptures were rigid and frontal, with no movement.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The Wrestler twists his torso, tenses his muscles and was made to be seen from every side: an astonishing exception for its time.
